narrative:
The model predicted a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year grades in law school had the strongest influence, pushing the prediction toward failure. You placed in the 4th decile, noticeably below the average of roughly 5.8 among students who were accepted. This weaker performance in a later, more advanced year signaled higher risk to the model.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked in your favor. At 38.5, you scored above the 37.2 average of accepted students, which helped pull the prediction toward passing. However, this positive effect was not large enough to overcome the concerns raised by your third-year performance.

Your first-year grades ranked third in influence and also nudged the outcome toward failure. Although your 6th-decile ranking matched the average of accepted students, the model still viewed it as a modest negative signal when combined with your later academic record.

Taken together, these academic indicators outweighed your strong undergraduate GPA of 3.5, upper-middle family income, and plan to attend full-time, all of which were typical or better than most accepted applicants.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record in any remaining law school work, consider retaking the LSAT if possible, or explore schools with different admissions thresholds. You may also want to speak with an admissions counselor about how to best present your full profile. (248 words)
